newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Slide in South African rand set to slow.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Slide in South African rand set to slow.

text.p: The rand's depreciation against the dollar is expected to slow next year and the currency could even appreciate slightly, results of a Reuters survey of 28 economists show.
They forecast the exchange rate would weaken to 4.92 against the dollar by the end of 1997, before falling to 5.17 by the end of the following year.
The consensus 1997 view was drawn from a wide 4.42 to 5.40 range.
One-year forward rates are currently at around 50 points, which translates into an exchange rate of about 5.20 against the dollar 12 months from now.

Economists who predicted the exchange rate would stabilise and possibly even appreciate slightly against the dollar next year, felt that the rand's 30 percent devaluation on the dollar in 1996 had left it at worst at fair value to the dollar.

"I think the fact that we are seeing the rand stabilising for longer periods at certain levels indicates that maybe the downward pressure has run out of steam," Huysamer Stals economist Johan Rossouw said.
"On a fundamental basis it is clearly undervalued. The question is just when will it start making headway again and to what extent."

Bureau for Economic Research economist Pieter Laubscher said that while there had been a number of fundamental reasons for the rand's depreciation in 1996, he believed the fall to a record low of 4.77 in October had been an overshoot.
"We calculated purchasing power parity and found a level of 4.45 being a fair value for 1997," he said.
Edey Rogers & Co strategic economist Edward Osborn said he expected the rand to weaken in line with inflation differentials of about seven percent next year.

"I have assumed that the adjustments that have taken place this year have cleared out the overvaluation of the rand and we should now be back on course in terms of a lower weakening of the rand against the dollar," Osborn said.

But while the underlying picture should be of weakening in line with inflation differentials, the currency could remain vulnerable to speculative attacks, according to Anastasia Gekis, economist at ABN AMRO.
"It is going to be volatile over the next two years, particularly if we don't get rid of exchange controls," she said.
Hania Farhan, economist at ING Barings, said she had added a risk premium to the inflation differential which could result in the rand weakening by a further 13 percent next year.
"One of the factors is the uncertainty about the timetable of exchange control lifting," Farhan said.
"The other is that while exchange controls remain, there is an emerging currency risk premium on top of the depreciation warranted by inflation differentials."
Farhan estimated the premium at between three and five percent.
